title: Why do some people criticize the Ministry of Repentance and Holiness?
dek: Prosperity preaching refused, a narrow road preached, and a ministry told it is too strict. What the criticism actually consists of, what Scripture says about testing it — and why “they opposed Jesus too” is not, by itself, an answer.
body:
The Ministry of Repentance and Holiness is known for a clear and uncompromising message: **repentance, holiness, the fear of God, and preparation for the return of Jesus Christ.**

Unlike ministries that place material prosperity at the centre of Christianity, it strongly emphasises turning away from sin and living according to God's Word. For some people that message is welcome. For others it can seem too strict, or controversial.

So why do some people criticize the Ministry of Repentance and Holiness?

There is no single answer. People may disagree with its interpretation of Scripture, its standards of holiness, its leadership, or particular teachings and practices. Others may simply find a message centred on repentance uncomfortable.

The ministry also sees a biblical pattern in which messages that confront sin and religious expectation attract opposition.

## A message that confronts the world

One reason the ministry stands out is its rejection of prosperity-centred Christianity.

Jesus warned:

> No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
> — Matthew 6:24, KJV

Paul warned in the same direction against those who treated godliness as a means of financial gain:

> Supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.
> — 1 Timothy 6:5, KJV

The emphasis of the ministry is therefore not primarily *"What can God give me?"* but **"How should I live before God?"**

That kind of preaching is uncomfortable, because repentance demands change. It asks what must be surrendered, what sin must be abandoned, and whether a person is truly living according to Christ's teaching. What that call actually involves is set out in [what repentance and holiness are](/articles/what-is-repentance-and-holiness).

## Jesus was also opposed by religious leaders

There is an important reality in the ministry of Jesus: **He was repeatedly challenged by religious leaders.**

The Pharisees questioned Him when He kept company with sinners:

> Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?
> — Matthew 9:11, KJV

Jesus answered:

> They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.
> — Matthew 9:12, KJV

Jesus did not avoid sinners, and He did not tell them they had no need to change. His mercy and His call to repentance went together.

That matters when considering a ministry centred on repentance. **Repentance is not hatred of sinners. It is the call to turn from sin and return to God.**

Jesus also confronted the religious establishment where outward religion had come loose from the heart:

> This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.
> — Matthew 15:8, KJV

And of the Pharisees:

> Even so ye also outwardly appear righteous unto men, but within ye are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.
> — Matthew 23:28, KJV

::note A warning that cuts both ways
:: The same verses that answer a critic can be turned on the ministry being defended. Jesus did not reserve those words for people outside the religious life; He said them to the most scrupulous keepers of the standard in Israel. Any ministry that emphasises holiness has to hear them as addressed to itself first — true holiness must involve the heart, not merely outward rules.

## Being unpopular does not automatically mean being right

Jesus' teaching was not always popular. In John 6, many of His disciples walked away after a hard saying:

> From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him.
> — John 6:66, KJV

He did not change the message to keep the crowd.

That teaches a principle worth holding carefully: **popularity is not the standard of truth.** A message can be unpopular and true. It can equally be unpopular and false. The question is never how many walked away; it is whether the message agrees with Scripture.

## Not every criticism is persecution

This distinction matters a great deal.

It would be easy for any ministry to say, *"People criticize us because we preach the truth."* But Scripture tells believers to examine what they hear.

Paul wrote:

> Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
> — 1 Thessalonians 5:21, KJV

The Bereans were praised for exactly this — they listened to Paul's preaching and then went to the Scriptures to see whether it was so:

> They received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
> — Acts 17:11, KJV

So criticism should neither be swallowed whole nor waved away. A person should not reject a ministry simply because it is criticized. Neither should a person accept everything a ministry teaches simply because it says it is being persecuted. **The standard is Scripture.**

## Why does a message about holiness attract criticism?

A message about holiness is difficult because it does not only offer comfort. It asks for a response.

Jesus described the Christian life as a narrow road:

> Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction.
> — Matthew 7:13, KJV

> Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life.
> — Matthew 7:14, KJV

The Ministry of Repentance and Holiness lays heavy emphasis on that narrow way — how believers conduct themselves, how they speak, how they [dress](/articles/why-do-women-in-the-ministry-of-repentance-and-holiness-dress-that-way), how they treat others, how they handle money, and how they separate themselves from sinful practice.

Christians disagree about how particular biblical principles should be applied, and some of the criticism is exactly that kind of disagreement rather than hostility to the gospel. But the broader principle is not in dispute: **following Christ should produce a transformed life.** What that word means, and what it does not, is set out in [what "without holiness no man shall see the Lord" means](/articles/what-does-without-holiness-no-man-shall-see-the-lord-mean).

## So, why do people criticize the ministry?

There are several reasons, and they are not all the same kind of thing.

Some disagree with its interpretation of Scripture. Some consider its standards of holiness too strict. Some disagree with its leadership, or with particular teachings and practices. And some are simply uncomfortable with a message that keeps calling people to repent, to fear God, to reject materialism, and to separate from sin.

The ministry may understand some of that opposition through the words of Jesus:

> If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
> — John 15:18, KJV

But the comparison has to be made carefully.

::note Being criticized does not make a ministry equivalent to Jesus
:: John 15:18 explains why the world opposes Christ. It does not certify that every ministry the world dislikes is therefore preaching Him. If opposition were proof of faithfulness, faithfulness could be manufactured by being disagreeable, and every teacher Scripture warns against would have the same defence available. Jesus is the standard by which every Christian ministry must measure itself, including this one.

## The better question

The real question is not whether the Ministry of Repentance and Holiness is criticized.

The better questions are these. What does it teach? Does that teaching agree with Scripture? Does its emphasis on holiness produce humility, love, repentance and obedience to Christ? Can what it teaches withstand honest examination?

Those are far more useful questions than whether people like the ministry.

The Bereans are the right example: they listened, they searched the Scriptures, and they tested what they were taught — and Luke calls them noble for it, not rebellious.

A ministry preaching repentance should not fear honest examination. A ministry preaching holiness should be willing to examine itself. And a ministry preaching truth should be able to say: **"Show me from Scripture."**

Criticism will always exist. The goal is not to silence every critic. It is to remain faithful to Christ, faithful to Scripture, and humble enough to let the truth stand on its own.

## Sources

Scripture quotations are from the King James Version, which is in the public domain. The description of the ministry's emphasis reflects what it publicly and consistently preaches; for its own statement of its teaching, consult its official channels. This page does not answer any particular published criticism, and nothing here should be read as a response to a named individual.
